Photoexcited Palladium-Catalyzed Synthesis of Chiral Allenes from
Alkynes via Isomerization and Deracemization Sequence
Changhua Song and Shouyun Yu*
Cite This: ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 15997−16002
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A photoexcited palladium-catalyzed synthesis of
chiral allenes from alkynes via a sequence of isomerization and
deracemization is disclosed. This method offers an efficient and
cost-effective approach to produce a wide range of chiral allenes
with good enantioselectivities and yields (up to 98% yield and 99%
ee). The use of readily available and stable alkynes as starting
materials simplifies experimental procedures and broadens the
scope of the chiral allene synthesis. DBU plays a crucial dual role in
this reaction to effectively facilitate the isomerization of alkynes to
allenes and enhance the palladium-catalyzed deracemization under
visible light excitation, both of which are vital for the success of the
process.
KEYWORDS: alkynes, allenes, deracemization, isomerization, palladium
■
INTRODUCTION
Allenes are molecules with unique reactivity patterns and are
widely utilized as building blocks for the synthesis of complex
molecules, including natural products and bioactive com-
pounds.
1
They can serve as enzyme inhibitors or antiviral
agents,
2
and chiral allenes also function as ligands in
asymmetric synthesis (Figure 1a).
3
Additionally, the axial-to-
central chirality transfer in chiral allenes, which creates new
stereogenic centers, has garnered significant interest among
organic and medicinal chemists.
4
Despite the broad explora-
tion of chiral allene applications, the asymmetric synthesis of
these valuable molecules remains a challenging task.
Alkynes, as isomers of allenes, are frequently employed as
starting materials for allene synthesis.
5
The isomerization of
alkynes to allenes via 1,3-prototropic rearrangement under
basic conditions remains one of the most direct and
convenient methods.
5b
However, achieving enantioenriched
chiral allenes through this strategy remains a significant
challenge (Figure 1b). In 2000, Shioiri and co-workers
reported an asymmetric isomerization of 1,3-diarylalkyne to
axially chiral allene in the presence of a phase-transfer catalyst.
6
Although the enantioselectivity of the reaction was moderate, it
represents an early example of constructing chiral allenes
through alkyne isomerization. In 2009, Tan and co-workers
demonstrated the Brønsted base-catalyzed isomerization
reaction of alkynes to chiral disubstituted allenes with high
enantioselectivity
7
where a bulky ester group was crucial for
achieving this selectivity. In 2011, Takemoto and co-workers
designed hydrogen-bond-donor catalysts that facilitated the
enantioselective isomerization of alkynyl amides to their
corresponding allenes.
8
More recently, in 2019, Kanai’s
group developed a Cu-catalyzed proton migration of skipped
enynes to allenes with good regio- and enantioselectivity.
9
Despite these advances, significant challenges remain in the
asymmetric isomerization of alkynes to chiral allenes: (1) the
conversion rates are often suboptimal, and the similar polarity
of alkynes and allenes complicates purification, and (2)
substrates typically require preinstalled polar functional groups
as binding sites, which limits the structural diversity. Therefore,
there is a pressing need for a method that delivers high
conversion rates and enantioselectivity, does not rely on
specific functional groups, and is applicable to a broad range of
substrates.
Very recently, our group successfully achieved the photo-
excited palladium-catalyzed deracemization of nonprefunction-
alized disubstituted allenes
10,11
by highlighting a significant
base effect that enhances enantioinduction. This success,
coupled with the fact that alkynes can isomerize to allenes
under basic conditions,
5
has inspired us to explore the use of
readily available and stable alkynes as starting materials for the
one-pot synthesis of chiral allenes. In this process, we envision
the base playing a dual role: facilitating the conversion of
alkynes to racemic allenes and enhancing the stereoselectivity

of the deracemization process (Figure 1c). Starting directly
from alkynes, without the need to presynthesize racemic
allenes, can significantly simplify experimental procedures and
broaden the scope of chiral allene synthesis.
Ene-allenes are versatile building blocks in organic synthesis
extensively used in electrocyclization and cycloaddition
reactions.
1a−f
Chiral ene-allenes are particularly valuable as
they enable the conversion of axial chirality to central chirality
through cycloisomerization.
4b
However, the asymmetric syn-
thesis of ene-allenes was rarely reported
9
and typically
depended on chiral substrates as starting materials.
12
Recognizing the importance of chiral ene-allenes, we selected
ene-alkyne 1a as a model substrate to construct ene-allene 2a
using the conditions we recently developed for allene
deracemization. Our goal of this study was to achieve the
conversion of alkynes to allenes while enhancing the
stereoselectivity of the deracemization process using a single
base.
■
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Ene-alkyne 1a was subjected to our optimized conditions for
the allene deracemization.

one-pot reaction. When KOH was then used as the base,

N
was used (entry 3). Identifying a base that can both effectively
promote the isomerization of alkynes to allenes and enhance
the stereoselectivity of the deracemization process proved
challenging. After extensive screening of bases (for more
information, see Table S3 in the Supporting Information), we
were pleased to find that DBU was the suitable choice. The
chiral ene-allene 2a was obtained in almost quantitative yield
(>99% GC yield, 98% isolated yield) and excellent
enantioselectivity (93% ee, entry 4). Other diphosphine
ligands, such as MeO-BIPHEP (L2), SEGPHOS (L3), and
GARPHOS (L4), did not yield better results (entries 5−7).
The effects of various solvents were also explored. The use of
dimethylacetamide (DMA), THF, and ethyl acetate (EA)
resulted in unchanged reaction yields but significantly
decreased enantiomeric excess (entries 8−10). Changing the
wavelength of the light source to 456 nm did not affect the
yield but reduced the enantiomeric excess (entry 11). In
comparison to 427 nm LEDs, the emission spectrum of 456
nm LEDs exhibited less overlap with the absorption spectrum
of the Pd/L/allene complex, resulting in a reduced
deracemization efficiency. In the absence of light, palladium,
or ligand, only racemic allenes were obtained (entries 12 and
13), suggesting that the reaction likely first produces racemic
allenes, which then undergo deracemization to yield

enantioenriched allenes. Without DBU, the alkyne was fully
recovered, and no allene formation was detected (entry 14).
Having identified the optimal reaction conditions, we
investigate the generality of our protocol (Figure 2). We
were pleased to report that aryl-vinyl disubstituted allenes
exhibit good yields (82−98%) and enantioselectivities (88−
93% ee). Both internal (2a) and terminal (2b−2e) ene-alkynes
yielded good results. Alkyl-vinyl disubstituted allenes (2f, 94%,
83% ee) were also compatible with our reaction system. Aryl-
alkyl disubstituted allenes (2g−2o) provided good yields (87−
95%) and good enantioselectivities (80−99% ee). Structures
bearing alkoxy groups (2g, 2h), tertiary amines (2i−2l),
substituted phenyl rings (2m, 2n), and aromatic heterocycles
(2o) produced favorable results. Utilizing this strategy, aryl−
aryl disubstituted allenes (2p−2x) also delivered excellent
yields (87−95%) and stereoselectivities (84−95% ee).

Common functional groups, such as methyl (2q), unprotected
hydroxyl (2r), bulky tert-butyl (2w), and halides (2x), were all
compatible with this reaction system, demonstrating remark-
able functional group tolerance. The heteroaromatic group,
such as thiophene (2u), proved to be a competent reaction
partner. Substituents at different positions (2s, 2t) and number
(2v) on the aryl rings of aryl−aryl disubstituted allenes were
well tolerated. In exploring the broad utility of this procedure,
we were delighted to observe that a series of complex
substrates derived from aspirin (2y), erlotinib (2z), indome-
tacin (2za), and isoxepac (2zb) could be transformed to the
desired products with excellent stereoselectivities. The reaction
could be scaled up to 4.5 mmol (1a) without affecting the yield
(97%) and enantioselectivity (93% ee). Disappointingly, the
synthesis of trisubstituted chiral allenes under standard
conditions was unsuccessful (for more unsuccessful substrates,
see Scheme S1 in the Supporting Information).
To validate the role of the base, we conducted kinetic
experiments and monitored the reaction’s progress (Figure 3).
We observed that both the yield and enantiomeric excess (ee)
of the allenes increased over time (Figure 3a). The presence of
DBU significantly accelerates the conversion of alkyne 1a to
allenes 2a with a notable 68% yield of 2a achieved in just 30
min and full conversion to the allene occurring within 2 h.
However, the rate of the allene deracemization lags behind the
alkyne isomerization with only 22% ee detected at 30 min and
its maximum being reached after 3 h. To further elucidate the
function of DBU, we plotted the time-dependent deracemiza-
tion curve of allene rac-2a (Figure 3b). Under standard
conditions, the enantiomeric excess of the racemic allene
peaked within 2 h. Additionally, excluding DBU from the
reaction resulted in a decrease in both the rate and extent of
deracemization. These findings suggest that DBU plays a dual
role: promoting the conversion of alkynes to allenes and
facilitating enantioenrichment of racemic chiral allenes, both of
which are essential for achieving high yields and stereo-
selectivity of this one-pot reaction. (For a detailed possible
reaction mechanism, see Scheme S3 in the Supporting
Information).
To further demonstrate the practicality of this method and
the versatility of substrates, we thoroughly investigated
different alkyne isomers (Figure 4a). We found that aryl-
alkenyl (2d) and aryl−aryl disubstituted allenes (2s) could be
obtained with good yields and enantioselectivity, even when
different alkyne precursors were used. Alkyne (1g′) with a
weakly acidic hydrogen atom could not isomerize to allene
(2g) under basic conditions, resulting in complete recovery of
starting material 1g′. The synthetic potentials of the alkenyl
allenes (2a) were demonstrated via hetero-Diels−Alder
reactions with diethyl azodicarboxylates and 4-phenyl-1,2,4-
triazoline-3,5-dione (PTAD)
13
to afford bicyclic products 3
and 4 (Figure 4b). Throughout the conversion from axial to
central chirality, the chirality was well maintained.
■
CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have reported successful isomerization and
deracemization from alkynes to chiral allenes with high yields
and enantioselectivity. DBU exhibits a critical dual catalytic
effect to efficiently facilitate the isomerization of alkynes into
allenes and accelerate the palladium-catalyzed deracemization
of allenes under visible light excitation, which is crucial for the
success of this one-pot reaction. By employing a strategy of
visible-light-induced palladium catalysis, a variety of disub-
stituted allenes, such as aryl-vinyl, alkyl-vinyl, aryl-alkyl, and
aryl−aryl, have been successfully constructed. Utilizing stable
and readily available alkynes as starting materials, we achieved
an efficient asymmetric transformation, overcoming the
challenges of low conversion rates and high substrate structure
sensitivity that were prevalent in previous transformations.
This method provides a new pathway for the synthesis of chiral
allenes, characterized by its universality and broad adaptability.

METHODS
General Procedure for Photoexcited Palladium-
Catalyzed Synthesis of Chiral Allenes from Alkynes. In
a nitrogen-filled glovebox, an 8 mL screw-cap test tube
equipped with a magnetic stir bar was charged with Pd
2
(dba)
3
(2.3 mg, 0.0025 mmol, 2.5 mol %), L1 (6.2 mg, 0.006 mmol, 6
mol %), and anhydrous DMSO (1.0 mL), and the mixture was
stirred for 10 min. Alkyne 1 (0.1 mmol), DBU (22.8 mg, 0.15
mmol), and anhydrous DMSO (1.0 mL) were added
sequentially. The reaction tube was sealed with a Teflon
screw cap and removed from the glovebox. The reaction
mixture was stirred vigorously under blue LEDs (427 nm) at
30 °C (the temperature was maintained in a water bath) for
the indicated reaction time. The reaction mixture was then
transferred to a 100 mL separatory funnel, rinsed/diluted with
20 mL ether, and washed with 20 mL of deionized water
(twice) and finally 20 mL of brine. The organic phase was
concentrated under vacuum and purified by chromatography
to afford chiral allene 2.
